sections.h2: Can farm or woodland be taxed below market value in North Carolina?
sections.html:
Yes. Qualifying agricultural, horticultural and forest acreage may be taxed at its present-use value, a figure based on what the land produces rather than what a developer might pay. The classes are defined in NCGS 105-277.3, and the owner must ask for the treatment.

Present-use classes and their minimums
ClassAcreage in actual productionOther test
Agricultural10 acres; an aquatic species farm needs 5 acres or 20,000 pounds sold yearlyGross income averaging at least $1,000 over the three years before January 1
Horticultural5 acresThe same $1,000 average, with a separate minimum for Christmas tree land
Forestland20 acres outside any farm unitA written forest management plan

Ownership counts too. The land must be the owner's home site, or have been held by the owner or a relative for the four years before January 1, or have come from an entity or trust that already held the classification.

sections.h2: What does a farm owner file to get present-use value?
sections.html:
An application goes to the assessor of the county where the land lies. NCGS 105-277.4 sets these windows.

  • First-time filers apply in the regular listing period, or within 30 days of a notice showing a changed value.
  • Later years need no new form unless the land is transferred or drops out through a change of use or acreage.
  • A buyer files within 60 days of the transfer date, and the form can go in any time in that calendar year.
  • Late forms need good cause, are approved by the county board, and help only for that calendar year's tax.

A disqualification notice must state the parcel number, the reason and the date of decision. The owner then has 60 days to appeal to the county board, with the Property Tax Commission as the next stop.

sections.h2: What happens to the tax savings when use-value land is sold?
sections.html:
The savings are deferred, not forgiven. The gap between present-use tax and full-value tax is carried on the books as a lien against the land. A disqualifying event makes the deferred amounts for the preceding three fiscal years payable (NCGS 105-277.4(c)).

A buyer who wants to keep the classification has a path under subsection (b2) of G.S. 105-277.3. The land must have been at present-use value when title passed, the buyer must keep the same use, file on time, and certify acceptance of the deferred tax liability. Miss one of those and the deferred taxes fall due.

  • A conveyance to a government unit or qualifying nonprofit at or under present-use value wipes out the deferred lien.
  • A conveyance above present-use value makes a share due, set by a fraction printed in the statute, with the sale price less present-use value on top and true value less present-use value below.
  • Land that leaves only because of enrollment in the federal Conservation Reserve Program owes nothing deferred.

Get the deferred balance from the assessor in writing before you list, then hand a copy to your closing attorney.

sections.h2: How does a county judge whether farmland is managed well enough?
sections.html:
The statute asks for a sound management program and lists ways to show one (NCGS 105-277.3(f)). An owner needs to show only one factor.

  • Enrollment in and compliance with an approved farm management plan.
  • Compliance with a set of best management practices, or with a minimum gross income per acre.
  • Evidence of net income from the operation, or that farming is the operator's main income.
  • Certification from a recognized agricultural agency in the county.

Forestland instead needs a written sound forest management plan for producing and selling forest products. A farm operator who meets the tests keeps the classification even when the owner collects rent rather than farming personally. Land under a qualifying conservation easement can also stay classified without production or income tests, provided the owner received no more than 75 percent of the donated interest's market value.

sections.h2: Which deadlines on a North Carolina tax bill matter most?
sections.html:
• September 1: bill due. Face-value payment is allowed through January 5.
  • January 6 and after: two percent interest, rising by three-fourths of one percent for each month or part of a month beginning February 1 (NCGS 105-360).
  • Postmark rule: a mailed payment counts on the day it was postmarked.
  • Early-payment discount: allowed only where the county or town adopted a schedule by resolution before May 1 and the Department of Revenue approved it.

Phone the tax office for the discount schedule, if any, and for the exact balance before you send money.

sections.h2: Who is billed if the house sells partway through the year?
sections.html:
Whoever held title on January 1 is listed and billed (NCGS 105-285). Close in March and the bill still arrives in the seller's name. Put the division in the contract, and have it appear on the settlement statement.

One exception covers land exempt on January 1, such as property bought from a government body before July 1. The buyer lists it as of the acquisition date, at its January 1 true value, and it is taxed for the fiscal year starting that July 1.

Assessors measure value as market value, the price a willing buyer and seller would agree on without pressure (NCGS 105-283), and reappraisal happens at least every eighth year (NCGS 105-286). An older appraisal date can leave your notice out of step with recent sales.

sections.h2: How do I dispute a value, and what relief might lower my bill?
sections.html:
Ask the county board of equalization and review for a hearing before it adjourns (NCGS 105-322). If you lose, a written notice to the Property Tax Commission has to arrive within 30 days of the board's mailed decision (NCGS 105-290). Bring comparable sales and repair estimates.

Homestead-type relief is applied for with the county assessor on Form AV-9 (NCDOR), and only one program may be used by an owner.

  • Age 65 or disability: the greater of $25,000 or half the appraised value is excluded (NCGS 105-277.1).
  • Disabled veteran: the first $45,000 is excluded, with no age or income test (NCGS 105-277.1C).
  • Circuit breaker: tax is capped at a share of income and the excess is deferred (NCGS 105-277.1B). The previous three years of deferral come due on a transfer.

sections.h2: Can I recover tax that was billed in error?
sections.html:
If the cause is a clerical error, an illegal tax or a levy for an illegal purpose, send a written demand to the taxing unit's governing body (NCGS 105-381). A refund demand may follow payment by up to five years from the due date or six months from payment, whichever ends later.

The body has 90 days to answer. A refusal or silence opens a three-year window to sue the taxing unit, and a winning judgment carries 6 percent interest plus costs.

sections.h2: What if tax is still owed at closing?
sections.html:
The lien stays with the parcel. It attaches as of the listing date together with penalties, interest and costs (NCGS 105-355). If a county enforces it, the vehicle is a civil action resembling a mortgage foreclosure (NCGS 105-374), ending in an auction at the courthouse door.

Redemption is open until confirmation if the person pays the taxes, penalties, interest and costs. Get a payoff figure from the tax collector for the closing attorney.

faqs.q: What does present-use value mean on a North Carolina tax bill?
faqs.a: It means qualifying farm, horticultural or forest land is valued on its current use. The owner applies with the county assessor, and the tax difference is carried as a deferred lien.

faqs.q: How much land must be in production to qualify?
faqs.a: Ten acres for agricultural land, five for horticultural land, and twenty for forestland. Aquatic farms follow a five-acre or 20,000-pound test, and the income test averages $1,000 over three years.

faqs.q: Do deferred taxes vanish at a sale of farmland?
faqs.a: No. The deferred tax for the preceding three fiscal years is due after a disqualifying event. A buyer who continues the use and accepts the liability in a timely application can keep the classification.

faqs.q: On what date does interest start on an unpaid bill?
faqs.a: January 6. A bill paid through January 5 costs face value, then two percent applies until February 1 and three-fourths of one percent per month follows.

faqs.q: Which party gets the bill when I sell in the middle of the year?
faqs.a: The county lists whoever owned the parcel on January 1. The contract and settlement statement can shift the cost, so check the balance with the tax office.
